messages.content: I want to develop streaming code-switching speech recognition that generalizes to unseen language pairings without sacrificing monolingual accuracy.

The goal has three connected parts: recognition must work in a streaming setting, remain effective when speech switches languages, and generalize to language pairings not previously seen. At the same time, improvements for code-switching should not come at a substantial cost to recognition of monolingual speech.
What would count as an improvement specifically around a language switch?

The stated target is to reduce word error rate, or WER, within three words of switches by 15% relative to a matched multilingual baseline. That focuses the comparison on recognition close to a switch, rather than treating an overall WER improvement as sufficient evidence that the switch region improved.
Is that 15 percentage points off WER?

No. It is a 15% relative reduction. If the matched multilingual baseline has near-switch WER B, the target is a near-switch WER of at most 0.85 × B for the system being developed. The statement does not give a numerical value for B.
And “within three words” is the window used for that comparison?

Yes. The WER target concerns words within three words of a language switch. The requirement does not further specify a boundary-counting convention, so I would keep that wording rather than assume an additional rule about which words are included.
How does the unseen-pairings part fit in? Is doing well on familiar combinations enough?

No. Generalization to unseen language pairings is part of the goal, and evaluating unseen pairings is an explicit requirement. Performance on pairings already encountered would not, by itself, establish that part of the objective. The statement does not prescribe which unseen pairings to use or a separate numerical threshold for each pairing.
I also don't want to claim that code-switching gains are acceptable if ordinary monolingual recognition gets noticeably worse.

That is why the monolingual constraint matters. At matched streaming latency, monolingual WER degradation must remain below 0.5 percentage points. This is a percentage-point limit on the change in WER, not a 0.5% relative-change limit.
Does “without sacrificing monolingual accuracy” mean there can be no increase in monolingual WER at all?

The numerical requirement gives that phrase a more precise tolerance: monolingual WER degradation must be below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency. An increase smaller than that bound is not excluded by the stated criterion; an increase of 0.5 percentage points would not be below it.
Why is matched streaming latency mentioned with the monolingual constraint?

It makes the monolingual WER condition a like-for-like comparison in streaming responsiveness. The goal is not to preserve monolingual accuracy by silently allowing a slower streaming setting. No particular latency value is specified; the stated condition is that latency be matched for this comparison.
Should I treat the near-switch target and the monolingual limit as alternatives?

No. They are simultaneous requirements: seek the 15% relative WER reduction within three words of switches versus the matched multilingual baseline, evaluate unseen language pairings, and keep monolingual WER degradation below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency. Meeting one does not remove the others.
Does this already say how the recognizer should achieve those outcomes?

No. It states the development goal and the conditions for assessing it, not an architecture, training method, dataset, or completed result. A proposed method would still need to be assessed against the near-switch comparison, unseen-pairing evaluation, and monolingual constraint.
So the central concern is that a system might improve around switches but fail to carry that over to new language combinations?

That is one distinction the goal makes. Improvement near switches and generalization to unseen pairings are both important, and neither should be inferred automatically from the other. The goal also keeps monolingual accuracy in view, so the desired outcome is not merely better code-switching recognition in isolation.
Can I say the 15% improvement must hold separately for every unseen pairing?

That would add a condition not stated here. The requirement specifies a 15% relative reduction in WER within three words of switches against a matched multilingual baseline and separately requires evaluation of unseen pairings. It does not say whether the 15% figure is computed per pairing or across an aggregate.
Then I should be careful not to turn an evaluation requirement into a claim that the goal has already been met.

Exactly. These are targets and evaluation conditions, not reported outcomes. It would be accurate to say the intended streaming recognizer should generalize to unseen language pairings while achieving the specified near-switch WER reduction and staying under the monolingual degradation limit at matched streaming latency.
What training approach would you propose for the streaming recognizer?

I would propose training a chunkwise transducer with four elements: shared phoneme bottlenecks, switch-spliced augmentation, a boundary-weighted loss, and frozen-teacher monolingual distillation. It is a proposed way to pursue the code-switching and monolingual goals, not a claim that those goals have been achieved.
What does the chunkwise part contribute?

It makes processing speech in chunks part of the recognizer design, which fits the streaming requirement. The proposal does not specify a chunk size or latency, and calling a model chunkwise does not by itself establish performance at any particular streaming latency.
And what is meant by a shared phoneme bottleneck?

Conceptually, it is a phoneme-oriented intermediate representation shared across languages, rather than entirely separate representations for each language pairing. Sharing could give the recognizer a way to use speech-sound information across pairings. The proposal does not specify a phoneme inventory, the precise location of the bottleneck, or how that representation would be implemented.
Is the claim that the shared bottleneck will make unseen pairings work?

No—that would be an outcome to establish, not something guaranteed by the design. Sharing is a proposed means of encouraging transfer across languages. Whether it helps on unseen pairings remains an evaluation question.
Explain switch-spliced augmentation without assuming a particular dataset.

It means augmenting training with examples formed by splicing speech segments so that they contain language switches. Its role in the proposal is to expose the recognizer to switch-containing speech during training. The proposal does not specify the source segments, how splice points are chosen, or how many augmented examples to use.
So the augmentation and the bottleneck address different things?

Yes, conceptually. The shared phoneme bottlenecks concern what information the model can represent across languages; switch-spliced augmentation concerns the switch-containing examples it can learn from. They are complementary parts of one proposed training approach, not independently demonstrated fixes.
Where does the boundary-weighted loss come in?

It puts extra training emphasis on errors near a language-switch boundary. That directs attention toward the portion of code-switching speech the goal particularly cares about. No weighting formula, boundary width for the loss, or coefficient is specified in the proposal.
Should I assume that its boundary definition is exactly the three-word WER evaluation window?

No. The earlier goal specifies a WER comparison within three words of switches, but this proposal does not say that the loss uses that exact window. The evaluation region and a loss-weighting rule are distinct unless a particular implementation explicitly makes them the same.
What is frozen-teacher monolingual distillation meant to do?

It uses a teacher whose parameters stay fixed to provide a distillation signal for monolingual speech while the proposed recognizer is trained. Its intended role is to help preserve monolingual recognition as the model also learns to handle switches. It is not a guarantee that monolingual WER will stay within the required limit.
Does “frozen” mean the whole recognizer is frozen?

No. It describes the teacher during distillation: the teacher is not updated by that training signal. The proposal is still to train the chunkwise transducer. It does not specify the teacher’s architecture or the exact form of the distillation signal.
Would it be accurate to describe the four pieces as one training recipe rather than four results?

Yes. The chunkwise transducer is the proposed recognizer; the shared phoneme bottlenecks are a proposed shared representation; switch-spliced augmentation supplies switch-containing training examples; boundary-weighted loss emphasizes switch regions; and frozen-teacher monolingual distillation is intended to protect monolingual performance. Those descriptions explain their roles without implying that any component has already succeeded.
I don't want the explanation to sound as if spliced training examples are themselves evidence of generalization.

They are not. Switch-spliced augmentation is a training choice. Generalization to unseen language pairings must be evaluated; it cannot be inferred merely from the presence of augmented examples or a shared bottleneck.
Nor should the frozen teacher be presented as proof that monolingual accuracy is preserved.

Right. Distillation is the proposed safeguard, while monolingual WER at matched streaming latency is the relevant outcome to check. The proposal states how training would try to balance code-switching improvements with monolingual accuracy, but supplies no measured outcome.
What details are deliberately left open here?

Among other things, the proposal leaves open the transducer’s chunk configuration, the bottleneck implementation, the construction of spliced examples, the boundary-loss weights, and the teacher and distillation formulation. Filling in those details would turn this high-level proposal into a more specific method; none is fixed by the proposal as stated.

The question I want to resolve is whether shared phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting can improve switch recognition on unseen language pairs without exceeding a 0.5-point loss in monolingual WER.

That is an open question about both transfer and the monolingual trade-off. The two proposed features might help recognition around switches in unseen pairings, but the proposal alone cannot establish that they do—or that any improvement comes without too much monolingual WER degradation.
Why put those two features together in the question?

They address different aspects of the challenge. A shared phoneme bottleneck is intended to make speech-sound representations useful across languages, including combinations not seen during training. Boundary weighting is intended to focus learning on recognition near a switch. The question asks whether those intended effects can coexist with the monolingual accuracy constraint.
Is improvement on a language pairing the system has seen enough to answer it?
No. The question specifically concerns unseen pairs. Better switch recognition on familiar pairings would not, on its own, show that the improvement transfers to pairings that were not seen.
Does a shared bottleneck imply that transfer will happen?

No. Sharing a representation provides a rationale for possible transfer, not proof of it. The bottleneck could be relevant to unseen-pair recognition, but whether it actually improves switch recognition there remains to be determined.
What uncertainty does boundary weighting introduce?

It directs more emphasis toward switch boundaries, where the proposed system is meant to improve. The open issue is whether that emphasis improves recognition on unseen pairs without an unacceptable loss on monolingual speech. Its intended focus is not itself evidence that the balance works.
When I say a 0.5-point monolingual WER loss, what exactly is the unit?

It is 0.5 percentage points of WER, not a 0.5% relative change. The goal’s monolingual condition is stricter than merely not exceeding the number: degradation must stay below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency.
Could an improvement at switches settle the question even if monolingual WER rises past that limit?

No. The question joins the two conditions: improving switch recognition on unseen pairs and keeping monolingual WER loss within the stated bound. A switch-region gain alone would leave the monolingual part unanswered or unmet.
What if monolingual WER stays below the limit, but there is no switch improvement on unseen pairs?
That would satisfy the preservation side but not the improvement side of this question. Both matter; neither substitutes for the other.
Does this question claim the bottleneck and boundary weighting alone will cause any improvement?

No. It asks whether they can help; it does not report a result or establish a cause. They were proposed within a broader chunkwise-transducer training approach, so this wording should not be read as measured evidence about the individual contribution of either feature.
Should frozen-teacher monolingual distillation be treated as proof that the 0.5-point condition will hold?

No. In the proposal, distillation is intended to help preserve monolingual performance. The question remains whether the resulting recognition performance actually stays within the monolingual WER bound while improving switch recognition on unseen pairs.
And the streaming aspect still matters when interpreting monolingual WER?
Yes. The monolingual comparison is at matched streaming latency. Otherwise, a WER comparison could leave out a condition that is part of the goal for a streaming recognizer.
How narrowly should I interpret “switch recognition” here?

It refers to recognition around language switches, rather than monolingual recognition in general. The goal gives a specific near-switch WER target within three words of switches, relative to a matched multilingual baseline. This question does not add a new boundary definition or claim that target has been reached.
So the honest answer right now is not simply yes or no?

Right. The proposal gives reasons to ask whether shared phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting can achieve that balance, but no outcome is supplied. The question remains open: can they improve recognition around switches on unseen pairs while keeping monolingual WER degradation below 0.5 percentage points at matched streaming latency?

I want to state a testable hypothesis: phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting reduce unseen-pair switch-window WER by at least 15%, while distillation holds monolingual WER loss to no more than 0.5 points at matched latency.

That states two predicted outcomes, not observed results. The first attributes an at-least-15% reduction in switch-window WER on unseen language pairs to the phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting. The second predicts that distillation keeps monolingual WER degradation at or below 0.5 percentage points when latency is matched.
Does “at least 15%” include exactly 15%?

Yes. A reduction of exactly 15% meets “at least 15%”; a smaller reduction does not. In the context of the stated goal, the WER reduction is relative to a matched multilingual baseline, rather than a drop of 15 percentage points.
And “no more than 0.5 points” also includes exactly 0.5?

Yes. The hypothesis’s “at or below 0.5 percentage points” includes exactly 0.5. That is distinct from the goal’s requirement that monolingual WER degradation stay below 0.5 percentage points, which does not include equality.
I don't want that distinction to disappear just because both statements mention the same number.

It should remain explicit. The hypothesis predicts monolingual WER loss of ≤0.5 percentage points at matched latency; the goal sets a <0.5-percentage-point degradation limit at matched streaming latency. A result of exactly 0.5 would fit the hypothesis’s bound but not the goal’s stricter bound.
What does the unseen-pair qualifier apply to?

It applies to the predicted switch-window WER reduction: the hypothesis concerns language pairings that are unseen, not only pairings the recognizer has encountered. The monolingual clause is a separate prediction about WER loss at matched latency.
Should I describe the bottleneck and boundary weighting as having already produced that reduction?

No. “Reduce” here expresses the hypothesis being tested. There is no measured switch-window WER, comparison result, or demonstrated attribution in the statement. It predicts that those features will deliver the specified reduction on unseen pairs.
Is distillation being credited with the switch-window improvement too?

Not in this hypothesis. The switch-window reduction is attributed to phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting; distillation is associated with limiting monolingual WER loss. That division describes the hypothesis, not proof that the components have those effects.
What does matching latency protect against in the monolingual claim?

It keeps the WER comparison tied to the same latency condition. The hypothesis does not predict that monolingual accuracy can be preserved by allowing a slower recognizer. It gives no particular latency value, only the requirement that latency be matched.
Does this hypothesis specify how much each of the two switch-focused components contributes?

No. It predicts an outcome for phoneme bottlenecks and boundary weighting together. It does not assign a share of the at-least-15% reduction to either component individually or say that each would meet the target alone.
What is meant by “switch-window” in this context?

It denotes the region around a language switch whose recognition is being assessed. The goal specifies a WER measure within three words of switches. The hypothesis uses the shorter phrase “switch-window WER” and does not introduce a different window or a new counting rule.
Could I regard a sufficiently small monolingual loss as evidence that the unseen-pair prediction is true?

No. The predictions concern different outcomes. Keeping monolingual WER loss within the hypothesized bound would not establish an at-least-15% switch-window WER reduction on unseen pairs; that reduction would need its own comparison.
Likewise, the switch-window reduction wouldn't tell us whether distillation held monolingual loss within its bound.

Correct. The hypothesis couples a predicted unseen-pair switch-window gain with a predicted monolingual constraint, but success on one measure does not establish success on the other. Both are part of the proposed balance.
How would we test the question about unseen-pair switch recognition and monolingual WER?

The plan is to train on English–Spanish and English–Arabic, then test on held-out Spanish–Arabic against a matched baseline. We would ablate the phoneme bottlenecks, boundary weighting, and distillation, and compare switch-window WER and monolingual WER at fixed latency. This describes an evaluation to carry out, not a result.
What makes Spanish–Arabic an unseen pairing in that plan?

English–Spanish and English–Arabic are the training pairings; Spanish–Arabic is held out for testing. Spanish and Arabic each appear in a training pairing, but their pairing with each other is the one being evaluated as unseen.
So “unseen” doesn't mean the recognizer has never encountered Spanish or Arabic?

Correct. It refers to the Spanish–Arabic combination being held out, not to either language being wholly absent from training. That distinction is central to what this test can say about generalization.
Why compare with a matched baseline rather than just report Spanish–Arabic WER?

WER on its own would describe performance but not the improvement relative to a comparator. Testing against a matched baseline makes the switch-window comparison meaningful. The plan does not specify further baseline construction details, so those should not be assumed.
What exactly do we compare on the held-out pairing?

The specified recognition measure is switch-window WER: errors in the region around a language switch. Spanish–Arabic is the held-out pairing for that test. The broader goal defines its near-switch WER target within three words of switches; this plan does not add a different window definition.
And the monolingual WER comparison is part of the same plan?

Yes. The plan compares both switch-window and monolingual WER. That keeps the assessment from considering a gain on the held-out code-switching pairing in isolation from potential monolingual degradation.
What does fixed latency mean for interpreting those WER comparisons?

The comparisons are to be made at a fixed streaming latency, rather than allowing latency to change while comparing WER. The plan gives no numerical latency value. Fixing it keeps differences in recognition accuracy from being presented as though they were independent of a change in streaming responsiveness.
Is the fixed-latency condition only for the monolingual result?
The plan says to compare switch-window and monolingual WER at fixed latency, so it applies to the comparisons being made, not just to the monolingual measure.
How do the ablations help answer the question?

They provide comparisons with each named component omitted: the phoneme bottlenecks, boundary weighting, and distillation. Those comparisons can help assess how the proposed components relate to switch-window and monolingual WER. The plan does not report what any ablation will show.
Should an ablation of boundary weighting be understood as a separate test from ablating the bottleneck?

They are separately named ablation targets, so their absence can be examined rather than attributing every difference to the full approach as a whole. The plan does not specify a complete matrix of combined ablations or the exact training configuration of each variant.
Why include distillation in the ablations if the main question mentions bottlenecks and boundary weighting?

The main question also concerns avoiding excessive monolingual WER loss. Distillation is part of the proposed training approach for that side of the balance, so ablating it can help examine its relationship to monolingual WER while the same switch-window and monolingual comparisons are made.
Could we say in advance that removing distillation will worsen monolingual WER?

No. That is a possible outcome to examine, not an observation supplied by the plan. The reason to include the ablation is to make the contribution assessable, not to presume its direction or magnitude.
Does removing the bottleneck necessarily hurt Spanish–Arabic switch recognition?

Not necessarily. Comparing the ablated version with the proposed system is how we would find out whether the bottleneck is associated with a difference on the held-out pairing under this evaluation. The plan itself establishes no such difference.
I also don't want to confuse a test of unseen pairing with a test on an unseen language.

Then describe it as a held-out Spanish–Arabic pairing after training on English–Spanish and English–Arabic. That wording identifies exactly what is held out without suggesting that Spanish or Arabic is an entirely unseen language.
Does the plan say anything about the amount of training speech or how switches are annotated?

No. It names the training pairings, the held-out test pairing, the comparator, the three ablation targets, the two WER measures, and the fixed-latency condition. It does not specify data quantities, annotation procedures, or other experimental details.
Can the matched baseline be assumed to have a particular architecture?

Not from this plan. It requires a matched baseline for comparison but does not define its architecture or the matching procedure. Those details would need to be specified separately rather than inferred here.
If we observe a difference in switch-window WER, is that automatically enough to answer the whole question?

No. The question concerns improvement on an unseen pairing without exceeding the monolingual WER loss limit. The plan therefore calls for both switch-window and monolingual WER comparisons at fixed latency. A difference on one measure alone cannot resolve the balance between them.
How would you state the test in one sentence without implying that we have run it?

Train on English–Spanish and English–Arabic, evaluate held-out Spanish–Arabic against a matched baseline, ablate phoneme bottlenecks, boundary weighting, and distillation, and compare switch-window and monolingual WER at fixed latency.
Let's move to the SwitchHoldout-v1 ablations. What exactly are we running?

The activity is to run the SwitchHoldout-v1 ablations on held-out Spanish–Arabic and measure switch-window WER and monolingual WER against a matched baseline at 320-ms latency. That specifies the comparisons to make, not their outcomes.
Does the 320-ms value apply to both WER measures?

Yes. The switch-window and monolingual WER comparisons are both specified at 320-ms latency. The point is to assess recognition at the stated streaming latency rather than compare results obtained under different latency conditions.
And Spanish–Arabic is the held-out pairing here, not a new training pairing?
Correct. In this activity, Spanish–Arabic is the held-out pairing on which the ablations are run. Calling the pairing held out does not mean that Spanish and Arabic are each unseen languages.
Which components does “ablations” refer to?

In the stated plan for this activity, the named ablation targets are the phoneme bottlenecks, boundary weighting, and distillation. SwitchHoldout-v1 is the name of this ablation activity; it does not itself specify the outcome of removing any component.
What do we learn by measuring switch-window WER rather than only overall WER?

Switch-window WER keeps the assessment focused on recognition near language switches. An overall WER number alone would not tell us how the system performs in that particular region. The activity calls for measuring that region and comparing it against the matched baseline; it supplies no measured value yet.
What role does monolingual WER play in the same run?

It captures the other side of the trade-off: whether performance on monolingual speech changes while switch recognition is assessed. Measuring both at 320-ms latency allows the results to be considered together, without assuming that a switch-window gain implies monolingual accuracy was preserved.
Should I describe this as a comparison against a matched baseline for both metrics?

Yes. The activity says to measure switch-window and monolingual WER against a matched baseline at 320-ms latency. It does not give the baseline’s WER values or further details of how the baseline is constructed.
Can we already say that an ablation worsened Spanish–Arabic WER?

No. Running an ablation creates a comparison, but the activity states no result. We cannot say whether removing a bottleneck, boundary weighting, or distillation raises, lowers, or leaves WER unchanged until measurements are provided.
Does the name SwitchHoldout-v1 imply that this is a successful first version?
No. It identifies the ablation activity. The name does not establish success, a particular WER value, or any conclusion about generalization.
How does this activity bear on the hypothesis about unseen-pair switch recognition?

The held-out Spanish–Arabic switch-window comparison provides a way to evaluate that prediction on an unseen pairing. The ablations can help examine the roles of the proposed components. But the activity itself does not show whether switch-window WER improves, much less by any specified amount.
And how does it bear on the monolingual-loss prediction?

The monolingual WER comparison at 320-ms latency provides the corresponding measurement for that prediction. In particular, the distillation ablation can be compared on monolingual WER. No monolingual loss or preservation result is stated here.
I want to keep “at 320-ms latency” from sounding like a measured recognition result.

It is the latency condition for the WER comparisons, not a WER outcome. A precise description would say that SwitchHoldout-v1 measures switch-window and monolingual WER against a matched baseline at 320-ms latency, without attaching any unreported accuracy numbers.
Is there any basis yet for claiming the ablations identify which component caused an improvement?

Not yet. The ablations are intended to make component comparisons possible. This activity names what is being run and measured, but gives neither the comparisons’ results nor a conclusion about the cause of any change.
So for now the concrete activity is the held-out test, the ablations, and the two matched-latency WER measurements?

Yes: run the SwitchHoldout-v1 ablations on held-out Spanish–Arabic, and measure switch-window and monolingual WER against a matched baseline at 320-ms latency. Any claim about improvement or monolingual degradation would require the resulting measurements.
What WER measurements came out of SwitchHoldout-v1?
On held-out Spanish–Arabic, switch-window WER fell from 34.0% to 28.5%, reported as a 16.2% relative reduction. Monolingual WER rose from 12.0% to 12.3%. The comparisons were made at 320-ms latency.
Are the first two percentages a relative change, or the WER values themselves?

They are WER values: 34.0% for the matched baseline and 28.5% for the compared system on the held-out Spanish–Arabic switch window. The relative change between those values is 16.2%, rounded to one decimal place.
Can you walk through that calculation?

The absolute difference is 34.0% − 28.5% = 5.5 percentage points of WER. Dividing 5.5 by the starting WER of 34.0 gives approximately 0.1618, or 16.2% relative. The 5.5-percentage-point drop and the 16.2% relative drop describe the same change in different units.
What is the corresponding change in monolingual WER?

It rose by 0.3 percentage points, from 12.0% to 12.3%. That is a degradation in monolingual WER, even though it is much smaller in percentage-point terms than the switch-window WER decrease. Both figures are reported at 320-ms latency.
Should I call the monolingual change a 0.3% rise?
That phrasing could confuse a relative percent increase with a percentage-point increase. The clearest description is that monolingual WER rose by 0.3 percentage points, from 12.0% to 12.3%.
Is the 16.2% a reduction in overall Spanish–Arabic WER?

No. It is the reported relative reduction in switch-window WER on held-out Spanish–Arabic. These figures do not provide an overall Spanish–Arabic WER or establish the size of any change outside the switch window.
Does “held-out Spanish–Arabic” mean neither language appeared in training?
No. The pairing was held out. The training plan named English–Spanish and English–Arabic, so the result concerns Spanish and Arabic together as a held-out pairing, not two entirely unseen languages.
Should the monolingual WER figures be described as Spanish–Arabic WER too?

No. Spanish–Arabic identifies the held-out code-switching pairing for the switch-window result. The 12.0% and 12.3% figures are monolingual WER values; the evidence does not break them down by language.
What does the 320-ms latency tell us about the comparison?
It states the latency condition under which these WER values were compared. It is not a WER value, and the evidence does not report how the same systems would perform at another latency.
Can we attribute the 16.2% reduction specifically to the phoneme bottleneck?

Not from these figures alone. Although the activity involved ablations, the evidence here reports the matched switch-window and monolingual WER comparisons, not separate WER values for individual ablations. It therefore does not isolate the bottleneck’s contribution.
What about boundary weighting or distillation—do these numbers isolate either one's effect?

No. There are no component-specific ablation results in this evidence. The reported changes describe the compared systems’ WER at 320-ms latency; they do not say how much of either change is attributable to boundary weighting or distillation.
Can I generalize this result to every unseen language pairing?
The reported held-out pairing is Spanish–Arabic. These measurements show what was observed for that pairing under the stated comparison, not what would happen for every other unseen pairing.
Give me a compact statement of the evidence that keeps those limits clear.

At 320-ms latency, switch-window WER on held-out Spanish–Arabic decreased from 34.0% to 28.5% versus the matched baseline, a 16.2% relative reduction, while monolingual WER increased from 12.0% to 12.3%. The figures do not provide component-specific ablation outcomes or results for other held-out pairings.
Given the reported WER changes, what should we do with the full model?

Advance the full model to additional unseen-pair validation. The reason for that decision is the observed 16.2% relative improvement in switch-window WER, accompanied by a 0.3-percentage-point monolingual WER loss.
Why advance it for more validation rather than treat the result as the final answer?

The decision is to continue evaluating the full model, not to conclude that it generalizes across unseen pairings. The reported improvement is encouraging for the held-out pairing that was measured, but additional unseen-pair validation is still the next step named here.
What does “full model” distinguish in this decision?

It identifies the model with the proposed components together, rather than one of the component-ablated variants. The decision does not select an individual ablation or claim that the reported gain can be assigned to a single component.
State the two numbers in a way that doesn't mix up their units.

Switch-window WER improved by 16.2% relative to the matched baseline. Monolingual WER increased by 0.3 percentage points. The first is a relative WER improvement; the second is a percentage-point WER loss.
Does advancing the model mean we're ignoring the monolingual loss?

No. The 0.3-point monolingual WER loss is expressly part of the reason given for the decision, alongside the 16.2% relative switch-window improvement. Advancing to validation does not erase that trade-off.
Should I say we have proved the model works on unseen language pairs generally?

No. The decision calls for additional unseen-pair validation precisely as a further evaluation of the full model. It does not report outcomes for those additional pairings or establish performance across unseen pairs in general.
Does this decision specify which pairings to validate next?
No. It specifies additional unseen-pair validation but does not name the additional pairings or prescribe their number.
Is this a decision to change the architecture or training approach?
No change is specified. The decision is to advance the full model to further validation on unseen pairings, based on the reported switch-window improvement and monolingual loss.
What if I describe the 0.3-point figure as an improvement too?
That would reverse its meaning. It is a monolingual WER loss: monolingual WER rose by 0.3 percentage points. The improvement in the decision refers to switch-window WER, which fell by 16.2% relative.
Can I say the additional validation has already confirmed the result?
No. Advancing the full model to additional unseen-pair validation states what to do next; it does not say that validation has been completed or what it found.
How would you phrase the decision without overclaiming?

Advance the full model to additional unseen-pair validation, based on a 16.2% relative improvement in switch-window WER and a 0.3-percentage-point monolingual WER loss. Leave the results of that additional validation open.
Now that the full model is being advanced, what is the plan for additional unseen-pair validation?

After advancing the full model, add English–French training. Then compare switch-window and monolingual WER for the French–Arabic and French–Spanish evaluations with matched baselines at 320-ms latency. Those are planned comparisons, not reported results.
Is English–French something we train on, or another pairing we hold out?

It is added to training. French–Arabic and French–Spanish are the pairings named for the subsequent comparisons. Keeping those roles distinct matters: this plan introduces French through English–French training, then examines the pairings of French with Arabic and Spanish.
Why call French–Arabic and French–Spanish unseen pairings if French is in training?

“Unseen” refers to the pairings, not necessarily to every language in them. English–French training exposes the model to French in a different pairing; the proposed validation asks about French paired with Arabic and with Spanish. It does not describe French as a wholly unseen language.
Does adding English–French replace the English–Spanish and English–Arabic training from the earlier plan?
No replacement is specified. The instruction is to *add* English–French training. It does not say to remove the other training pairings or change their status.
Should we evaluate French–Arabic first and French–Spanish later?
